analysis.body:
The most detailed public accounting of AI use inside the United States federal government comes from GAO, which audited major federal agencies and found that twenty of twenty-three reported approximately 1,200 current and planned AI use cases. Only about 200 of those instances involved AI that agencies reported as currently in production, meaning the large majority of catalogued use cases remained in planning or earlier phases at the time of review. Three agencies reported having no uses for AI at all, while NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest numbers of use cases. The applications agencies described ranged from analyzing drone photographs and large datasets to identifying border activities through camera and radar feeds and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers.

GAO's review also found significant problems with how agencies track their own AI activity. Five agencies provided comprehensive information for each reported use case, while the other fifteen had instances of incomplete or inaccurate data, including missing required fields such as AI life cycle stage. Two agencies included uses that were later determined not to qualify as AI at all. Ten of twenty-three agencies fully implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, twelve implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. OMB had not yet developed government-wide guidance on acquiring and using AI, a gap GAO identified as preventing consistent management of AI risk across the federal government.

On the funding side, the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included 1.8 billion dollars for nondefense research and development investment in AI, according to GAO. The General Services Administration established an AI Center of Excellence and the Department of Commerce created a plan to develop AI technical standards, two of the more concrete institutional steps the audit identified. The Office of Personnel Management had not yet established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work, which GAO noted as an outstanding requirement.

Stanford HAI tracks the broader trajectory through its annual AI Index, which it describes as providing comprehensive, data-driven analysis of AI's technical progress, economic influence, and societal impact for policymakers and governments worldwide. The 2026 edition of the Index noted what Stanford HAI characterized as a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared governments are to manage it, with governance frameworks falling behind technical capability and investment. OECD.AI monitors the policy landscape across member and partner countries, giving access to more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives, while Oxford Insights publishes a Government AI Readiness Index that scores countries on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption as a standard cross-national comparison.

The legislative environment around government AI use is dense and fast-moving. Theworldofai.org tracks 2,425 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily, reflecting the scale of state-level legislative activity layered on top of federal executive orders and agency-specific requirements. For any organization or agency considering AI deployment in a public-sector context, the GAO findings suggest that the practical challenge is not only choosing the right technology but building the internal governance infrastructure, accurate inventories, clear acquisition guidance, and defined workforce roles, that federal requirements already demand and that most agencies have not yet fully delivered.
